title: The Chilling Effect of Strong Reactions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article describes how people who react defensively to feedback end up training everyone around them to stop giving it. Over time, hyper-sensitive colleagues create a 'chilling effect' where important information about performance, conflict, and disagreement never reaches them, which the author argues ultimately harms everyone involved. It distinguishes those who consciously use strong reactions to control what others say from those who are simply unaware of the pattern they've created. The recommended remedy is a sustained, coordinated effort: naming the pattern directly, warning that feedback will continue regardless of the reaction, and enlisting others to hold the same line consistently. The piece frames breaking this cycle as an unglamorous but essential leadership task.
points: Hyper-sensitive reactions to feedback train colleagues to filter or withhold information, creating a 'chilling effect' over time.
Some strong reactors consciously use their reactions to control what others will say to them; others are simply unaware of the pattern.
Leaders must confront the hyper-sensitive party directly, name the pattern, and commit to continuing honest feedback regardless of the reaction.
No single conversation fixes the dynamic - it requires sustained, repeated effort over time.
Coordinating with others to consistently push through discomfort is what ultimately weakens the chilling effect.
quotes: Some people are hyper-sensitive to just about any feedback or criticism.
Over time, their extreme reactions create a chilling effect on what they hear from others.
When the relationship rule of no or little feedback becomes established, everyone loses.
Walking on eggshells to avoid a strong reaction must become an unacceptable way to engage.
Giving someone feedback about how they receive feedback can be dicey, but that is the task at hand.
When it comes to those who handily reject all feedback, taking the chill off is what leaders do.
